title: Temporary links, private credentials
description: Understand signed media access and the difference between Vault and provider signing.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.

chapters.title: Keep long-lived credentials on the server

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional application showing a customer a recording. Should it put the Vault account secret in the browser?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. The storage endpoints use account credentials per request, and the guide explicitly says not to embed them in frontend code. A trusted backend obtains a temporary signed URL and shares that limited-lifetime link instead.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does a thumbnail need a completely different authentication system?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Recordings and generated assets use the same signed-access pattern with their respective filenames. Single-file and bulk endpoints support different retrieval needs. Use the documented contract rather than inventing asset names.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What does the returned link actually connect the customer to?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Provider signing lets the client download from storage directly. Vault signing has Vault validate the signature and stream the object. Providers can override the global signing mode, so different storage destinations can have different access paths.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the caveat for a replicated Vault?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Vault signing needs a stable signing key shared across replicas and a correctly configured public URL. Keep expiry and client reachability in mind. Test a real asset from the user's network, and use the linked examples for the exact response format and error handling.
